title: Microsoft Stocks Rise 0.26% as Code Red Targets One-Hour Outage Recovery - TradingView
content: Microsoft MSFT shares rose 0.26% to $491.18 at 10:55 a.m. ET on Friday, November 27, in the shortened regular session, as investors weighed an internal Code Red push to fix Microsoft 365 reliability. Memos reviewed by Reuters show the company wants to resolve future global incidents within an hour, a goal Microsoft 365 Core president Jason Henderson acknowledged it does not yet meet. The trigger was a nearly 24-hour outage on November 12 and 13 that knocked out Exchange Online, Outlook, Teams and Copilot. Microsoft's preliminary review traced it to a July fix for networking gateway servers and lock contention in an internal Windows process, leaving more than 80% of servers unresponsive at the worst point. Outage reports peaked at about 130,000 across 74 countries, TweakTown reported, and Satya Nadella apologized. The GuruFocus chart shows a perfect GF Score of 100/100, with elite profitability, a strong balance sheet and top-tier momentum. The GF Value of $606.32 implies a 19.0% discount, which GuruFocus rates modestly undervalued, so the market is not treating the outage as lasting damage. The commercial risk is real, though: Copilot is sold on top of Microsoft 365, and every hour of downtime weakens the case for charging enterprises more per seat. The next test is Microsoft's final post-incident report and whether commercial bookings hold up next quarter. Select market data provided by ICE Data Services. Coinbase pays us for certain activity generated through this link. Prices displayed are informational. A month has gone by since the last earnings report for Microsoft (MSFT). Shares have lost about 7.6% in that time frame, underperforming the S&P 500. But investors have to be wondering, will the recent negative trend continue leading up to its next earnings release, or is Microsoft due for a breakout? Well, first let's take a quick look at the latest earnings report in order to get a better handle on the recent drivers for Microsoft Corporation before we dive into how investors and analysts have reacted as of late. Microsoft (MSFT) reported first-quarter fiscal 2027 earnings of $4.89 per share on a non-GAAP basis (excluding OpenAI investment impacts), which increased 18% on a year-over-year basis (up 19% in constant currency). The figure beat the Zacks Consensus Estimate by 3.82%. On a GAAP basis, earnings per share were $4.92, up 32% year over year.Revenues of $92.3 billion increased 19% year over year (up 19% in constant currency) and beat the Zacks Consensus Estimate by 1.88%. The top line came above management's guided range of $89.85-$90.95 billion, with results exceeding the company's expectations across revenues, operating income and earnings per share.Microsoft Cloud revenues totaled $63.9 billion, up 30% year over year (31% in cc), accelerating from 27% growth in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026. Commercial remaining performance obligation reached $677 billion, up 73% year over year, with a weighted average duration of 2.3 years. Roughly 30% of this is expected to be recognized as revenue over the next 12 months, up 29% year over year, while the portion recognized beyond 12 months increased 98%. Commercial bookings declined 12% (down 11% in cc), reflecting large Azure commitments in the prior-year quarter, partly offset by a large Azure commitment signed this quarter.Beginning fiscal 2027, Microsoft reports results under two segments, Agents and Infra and Devices and Consumer, replacing the earlier three-segment structure. The change was announced in September 2026, and prior-period figures have been recast to conform to the new structure. Agents and InfraThe Agents and Infra segment generated $76.8 billion in revenue, which grew 25% year over year (25% in cc).Azure revenues surged 48% year over year (48% in cc) to $33.2 billion, accelerating from 42% growth in the prior quarter and ahead of the company's expectations, despite delays in some third-party capacity deliveries. Growth was driven by Foundry and improved CPU monetization. Foundry revenues more than tripled year over year, aided by efficiency gains across the GPU fleet that freed up additional capacity for customers, as well as higher revenue per token.Microsoft 365 Commercial cloud revenues increased 17% on a reported basis (18% in cc), or 18% (19% in cc) when adjusted for a prior-year comparable that had benefited from one point of in-period revenue recognition. Results were ahead of expectations on stronger GitHub Copilot adoption and usage, partially offset by weaker sales execution in Microsoft 365 E3 and stand-alone SKUs. Paid Microsoft 365 commercial seats grew 5%. Average revenue per user growth was led by premium offerings, including Microsoft 365 Copilot, E5 and E7, the latter of which has already reached millions of paid seats.Microsoft 365 Consumer cloud revenues rose 17% (16% in cc), as the business began lapping the benefit of the prior-year price increase. Total Microsoft 365 cloud revenues were $27.8 billion, up 17%.Productivity and server licensing revenues declined 3% (down 2% in cc) to $8.4 billion. Industry solutions cloud revenues grew 10%, driven by Dynamics 365 and LinkedIn Talent Solutions, although booking trends continued to moderate. Frontier and support services revenues rose 4% (5% in cc) to $2.1 billion.Operating income for the segment rose to $40.6 billion from $32.7 billion a year earlier, representing an increase of 24% (25% in cc). Operating margin decreased slightly to 53% as sales mix shifted toward Azure. Microsoft Cloud gross margin was 66%, down year over year.Devices and ConsumerThe Devices and Consumer segment generated $15.5 billion in revenues, down 3% year over year (down 3% in cc), pressured by a steep decline in Windows OEM and devices revenues, partly offset by growth in search and advertising.Search and advertising revenues, excluding traffic acquisition costs, rose 12%, ahead of expectations on higher volume and rate across LinkedIn, Edge and Bing. Xbox content and services revenues fell 2% (down 1% in cc), as declines in third-party content and Xbox Game Pass were partially offset by growth in first-party content. Windows OEM and devices revenues declined 22%, with Windows OEM revenues down 27% (down 28% in cc) due to a prior-year comparable that benefited from Windows 10 end of support, inventory drawdowns by OEM and channel partners, and weaker PC market demand.Operating income for the segment increased to $5.4 billion from $5.2 billion a year earlier, up 2% (3% in cc). Operating margin expanded to 35%, aided by lower amortization of intangible assets from the Activision acquisition. Microsoft announced its biggest Copilot update to date, combining Chat, Cowork, Autopilot and Code into a single unified experience across commercial and consumer users. Copilot daily users increased nearly 50% sequentially and more than five-fold year over year, while the number of customers with more than 50,000 Copilot seats rose more than eight-fold. Customers consuming Copilot credits through usage-based billing grew more than 75% in the quarter. The company did not provide an updated paid Copilot seat count this quarter.Foundry crossed 120,000 customers, and revenues from open-source models on Foundry increased 10-fold. Microsoft completed pre-training of MAI Base 2, its next first-party base model, and released DecisionOne, a structured decision-making model used by more than 4,000 customers in its first month. Paid Fabric customers reached 44,000, up more than 50% year over year, while more than 50 million agents are now registered in Agent 365, up over 30% sequentially.On GitHub, agent-generated pull requests increased six-fold over the past six months, and GitHub Advanced Security revenues grew more than 50% year over year. At GitHub Universe, the company announced broad availability of Copilot Fusion, which brings multi-model orchestration to software development.Microsoft added 24 new data centers across five continents during the quarter, cut dock-to-live times for new GB300 systems in its largest regions by about 20% sequentially and docked its first NVIDIA Vera Rubin GPUs. Its in-house Maia 200 chip is delivering up to 1.7 times more tokens per watt across Teams and Copilot workloads. LinkedIn surpassed 1.4 billion members, with time spent viewing feed content up 15% year over year. In gaming, Minecraft delivered a record quarter for engagement and revenues. The company also announced an employee voluntary exit offer, the estimated cost of which is included in its second-quarter guidance. Gross margin reached $62.6 billion, up 17% year over year, with gross margin percentage at 68%.Total operating expenses increased to $16.6 billion from $15.7 billion, up 6%, driven by continued investments in research and development, compute capacity and talent. Research and development expenses were $9 billion, sales and marketing were $5.7 billion, and general and administrative expenses were $1.9 billion.Operating income increased 21% year over year (22% in cc) to $45.9 billion, while operating margin expanded slightly to 50%. Net income reached $36.6 billion, up 32% on a GAAP basis. On a non-GAAP basis, excluding OpenAI-related impacts, net income was $36.4 billion, up 18% (19% in cc).Other income and expense, net, was a positive $38 million in the quarter compared with a negative $3.7 billion a year earlier. Excluding the impact of OpenAI investments, other income and expense was a negative $234 million. Capital expenditures, including finance leases, were $45.2 billion, below expectations as some anticipated third-party capacity deliveries were delayed. Roughly three-quarters of spending went toward short-lived assets, primarily CPUs and GPUs, including higher memory and storage costs. Finance leases were $7.4 billion, while cash paid for property and equipment was $39.4 billion.Cash flow from operations totaled $58 billion, up 29% year over year, driven by strong cloud billings and collections. Free cash flow was $18.6 billion, down from $25.7 billion a year ago, reflecting higher capital spending.As of Sept. 30, 2026, Microsoft had total cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments of $64.5 billion compared with $76.8 billion as of June 30, 2026. Long-term debt was $31.1 billion, with an additional $4.4 billion in the current portion of long-term debt.Microsoft returned $10.2 billion to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases during the fiscal first quarter. The fiscal first quarter reflected net gains from investments in OpenAI of $207 million, adding 3 cents to earnings per share. This compares with the first quarter of fiscal 2026, when net losses from OpenAI investments decreased net income and earnings per share by $3.1 billion and 41 cents, respectively.These OpenAI-related impacts have historically created volatility in reported GAAP results, leading the company to provide non-GAAP measures excluding these effects to help investors better understand operational performance. For the second quarter of fiscal 2027, Microsoft expects total revenues between $96 billion and $97.1 billion, indicating growth of 18% to 19%. Based on current rates, foreign currency is not expected to have a meaningful impact on revenues, cost of revenues or operating expense growth.The Agents and Infra segment is expected to generate revenues between $80.1 billion and $80.7 billion, indicating growth of 24% to 25%. Azure revenue growth is projected at 49% to 50% in cc, with demand continuing to exceed available supply and some third-party GPU capacity contracts delayed to the second half of the fiscal year. Microsoft 365 Commercial cloud revenues are expected to grow approximately 19% in cc, while Microsoft 365 Consumer cloud revenues are expected to grow in the low teens. Microsoft Cloud gross margin is expected to be roughly 65%.The Devices and Consumer segment is expected to generate revenues between $15.9 billion and $16.4 billion. Search and advertising revenue growth, excluding traffic acquisition costs, is expected in the low double digits, and Xbox content and services revenues are expected to grow in the mid-to-high single digits depending on the timing of first- and third-party content launches. Windows OEM and devices revenues are expected to decline in the mid-30s percentage range.Cost of revenues is projected between $32.7 billion and $32.9 billion, up 26% to 27%, while operating expenses are expected between $18.5 billion and $18.6 billion, up 9%. title: Can Microsoft Stock Sustain Margins as AI Data Center Spending Climbs? - The Globe and Mail
content: MicrosoftMSFT is testing how far AI data center spending can climb before it erodes profitability. Capital expenditures, including finance leases, reached $45.2 billion in the first quarter of fiscal 2027, with roughly three-fourths directed toward short-lived assets, primarily CPUs and GPUs. Cash paid for property and equipment was $39.4 billion compared with $19.4 billion in the year-ago quarter.So far, revenue momentum has absorbed the cost. First-quarter revenues rose 19% to $92.3 billion, while operating income grew 21% to $45.9 billion. Operating margin was 50%, up slightly year over year. Microsoft Cloud revenues climbed 30% to $63.9 billion, with Azure up 48%. Commercial remaining performance obligation jumped 73% to $677 billion, offering visibility to support the buildout.However, pressure is building beneath the headline. Microsoft Cloud gross margin was 66%, down year over year, and is expected to be roughly 65% in the second quarter. Second-quarter cost of revenues is guided in the range of $32.7-$32.9 billion, up 26-27%, whereas revenues are guided in the range of $96-$97.1 billion, up 18-19%. Operating expenses are projected at $18.5-$18.6 billion, up 9%, with cost guidance including an estimate for the voluntary exit offer. Consequently, operating margin is expected to decline slightly year over year.The spending curve is also steepening. Second-quarter capex is expected to exceed $50 billion, with calendar-year capex projected at approximately $170 billion. Spending should accelerate in the second half, primarily on CPUs, reflecting higher memory and storage costs, along with GPUs and delayed third-party capacity deliveries. Still, Microsoft expects to remain free cash flow positive in fiscal 2027.Custom silicon could ease part of the burden. In October 2026, Microsoft announced Maia 300, expected to deliver 40% more tokens per megawatt than leading GPU-based systems, with multi-gigawatt deployments beginning in 2027. Whether such efficiencies scale fast enough to offset rising infrastructure costs remains the key margin question. AmazonAMZN and Alphabet GOOGL both face similar trade-offs between AI capacity and profitability. Amazon expects 2026 cash capital expenditures of approximately $220 billion. Its AWS segment operating income rose to $17.8 billion in the third quarter from $11.4 billion in the year-ago quarter, as sales grew 39% to $46 billion. However, Amazon reported a trailing 12-month free cash flow outflow of $42.4 billion. Similarly, Alphabet maintained its 2026 capex guidance of $195-$205 billion after spending $51.4 billion in the third quarter. Meanwhile, Alphabet's Google Cloud revenues jumped 103% to $30.7 billion, with operating income climbing to $11.1 billion from $3.6 billion. MSFT shares have gained 1.8% in the year-to-date (YTD) period against the Zacks Computer – Software industry’s 9% decline. The Zacks Computer and Technology sector has declined 3.1% in the same time frame. From a valuation standpoint, MSFT stock appears overvalued, trading at a trailing 12-month price/earnings ratio of 27.16X, higher than the industry’s 24.95X. MSFT has a Value Score of C. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for MSFT’s fiscal 2027 earnings is pegged at $19.91 per share. The estimate indicates 10.9% year-over-year growth. Tech stocks have been hit hard this month as investors worry about the enormous amount of money being spent on artificial intelligence (AI), and Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) has been no exception. Shares are down about 13% from their all-time highs. But I think Microsoft is being unfairly punished here. While many big tech companies are free cash flow negative due to heavy AI spending, Microsoft has affirmed it will remain in the black at least through fiscal 2027. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » That's a big deal. And I think it's one reason why the tech sell-off in November presents an attractive buying opportunity for Microsoft before the end of 2026. Microsoft is one of the biggest players in the cloud computing space, holding 21% of the global cloud infrastructure market. That makes Azure the second-largest provider of cloud services behind Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN). In Microsoft's fiscal first quarter of 2027, which ended Sept. 30, Azure revenue increased 48% from the previous year. Total Microsoft Cloud revenue was $63.9 billion, up 30% from a year ago, and the company's commercial backlog reached $677 billion. That's an enormous amount of business coming down the line, so Microsoft is spending freely to ensure it has enough computing capacity to meet demand. It spent $45.2 billion on capex in the quarter. But even with that spending, free cash flow remained positive at $18.6 billion. That's because Microsoft generated $58 billion in operating cash flow during the quarter, up 29% from a year earlier. That's a big difference from some other tech companies whose AI spending has pushed free cash flow into negative territory. Despite concerns about AI spending, Microsoft's underlying business is performing very well, thanks to its well-known software business. Nearly 4 million companies use Microsoft 365, including its popular office programs such as Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and Outlook. Those subscriptions provide recurring revenue, while Microsoft's Copilot AI products provide opportunities to sell more services to existing customers. Microsoft 365 commercial cloud revenue increased 17% during the quarter. That helped Microsoft's fiscal first-quarter revenue increase 19% to $92.3 billion, while operating income climbed 21% to $45.9 billion. Net income was $36.6 billion, up 32% from a year ago. I don't expect Microsoft to slow its AI investments anytime soon -- and why should it? Microsoft Azure is generating substantial revenue, and Microsoft can continue to invest in the business while maintaining positive free cash flow. Now down 13% from its all-time high, Microsoft offers investors an opportunity to buy a highly profitable company with two powerful businesses -- cloud computing and productivity software. I think the market is overlooking Microsoft's ability to finance its AI ambitions, and it's an appealing opportunity for investors before year-end.
